text.p: Papua New Guinea gold miner Highlands Gold Ltd said on Tuesday it had appointed investment bank Rothschild Australia to help it find partners for the development work of two large mineral deposits.

The company said the Frieda River/Nena copper/gold deposit and the Ramu nickel/cobalt project had potential to be developed into mines within the decade but at a hefty cost of 3.0 billion kina (US$2.25 billion).
Highlands chairman Clive Hildebrand also told the annual meeting he hoped the company's share price would improve with continued development work on the joint venture projects.
Hildebrand said Highlands was seeking new farm-in partners to take each project through the feasibility stage and fund the company's share.
"The incoming parties will being the necessary technical, marketing, financial and management skills required for projects of this magnitude," he said at the Port Moresby meeting.

"Rothschild Australia Ltd has been appointed to assist us in securing the best commercial arrangements for the joint ventures so that the value of the projects is best reflected in our share price," he said.
Highlands has a 65 percent stake in the Ramu project, with Nord Pacific Ltd as a minority shareholder.
It has 84 percent control of Frieda/Nena with Japan's OMRD Frieda Co Ltd as minority partner.
Highlands is also a 25 percent partner in the one million ounce per year Porgera gold mine.
Hildebrand said directors were disappointed that the company's share price did not reflect its potential assets and they aimed to improve Highlands' standing in the share market.
MIM Holdings Ltd offloaded its 65 percent stake in Highlands earlier this year at a price of 65 cents per share.
Highlands shares were one cent lower at A$0.56 at 2.05 p.m. (0305 GMT).

Brisbane stockbroker Wilson HTM Ltd said in a report issued on Tuesday that Highlands was a buy and that the miner's share price did not reflect any upside from its Porgera investment or the two mineral joint ventures.
It said the cost of developing the projects was too large for Highlands, hence the need for partners.
"We believe that Highlands is significantly under-valued and has the potential for a major share price re-rating," it said.
